gloss_terse: Cosam, an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
gloss_readable: Cosam appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, positioned between Addi and Elmadam in the post-exilic lineage. Like many names in this section of Luke 3, historical details beyond the genealogical record are unknown. The name may derive from a Hebrew root, though its etymology remains uncertain.

senses.1: This proper name occurs once in Luke 3:28, part of the ascending genealogy that traces Jesus' lineage back to Adam. The multilingual evidence consistently treats this as a transliterated personal name, with slight variations in vocalization across language traditions reflecting different approaches to rendering Greek names.

gloss_terse: Lamech, patriarch in Jesus' genealogy from the line of Seth
gloss_readable: Lamech appears in Luke's genealogy as the father of Methuselah and descendant of Enosh. He is the same patriarch mentioned in Genesis 5:25-31, where he lived 777 years and fathered Noah. The Hebrew name (לֶמֶךְ) is transliterated into Greek as an indeclinable proper noun, maintaining its Semitic form.

senses.1: Occurring in Luke 3:36, this name links Jesus' genealogy to the ancient patriarchs between Adam and Noah. Cross-linguistic glosses show consistent recognition of this as the antediluvian patriarch, with transliterations preserving the distinctive guttural sound of the Hebrew original across European language traditions.

gloss_terse: brilliance, radiance, splendor (especially of light)
gloss_readable: This term denotes intense brightness or radiance, originally used in classical Greek for the brilliance of heavenly bodies, polished metals, or gleaming armor. In Acts 26:13, Paul describes the light that struck him on the Damascus road as exceeding the brightness of the midday sun. The word carries connotations of overwhelming visual intensity and supernatural glory.

senses.1: Paul uses this word in Acts 26:13 to convey that the heavenly light surpassed even the sun's brilliance at noon—the brightest natural reference point available. The multilingual glosses (brightness, resplandor, splendeur) consistently emphasize luminous intensity, reflecting the term's classical usage for radiant phenomena and its theological application to divine manifestation.

gloss_terse: splendidly, magnificently, sumptuously
gloss_readable: This adverb describes living or acting in a manner characterized by luxury, magnificence, or lavish display. In Luke 16:19, it modifies how the rich man feasted every day—not merely eating well, but indulging in extravagant, ostentatious consumption. The term evokes the lifestyle of the wealthy elite in the Greco-Roman world, where public display of wealth was a social marker.

senses.1: The sole New Testament occurrence (Luke 16:19) contrasts the rich man's daily splendid feasting with Lazarus' destitution at his gate. Cross-linguistic evidence (splendidly, espléndidamente, splendidement) uniformly captures the sense of luxurious excess, highlighting the moral dimensions of wealth disparity that Jesus addresses in the parable.

gloss_terse: hewn from rock, carved out of stone
gloss_readable: This adjective describes something cut or carved from solid rock, particularly tombs hewn into cliff faces or hillsides. In Luke 23:53, it characterizes the new tomb where Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus' body—a burial chamber carved entirely from stone, not constructed with masonry. Such rock-hewn tombs were prestigious burial sites in first-century Judea, requiring considerable expense and labor.

senses.1: Applied to Jesus' burial tomb in Luke 23:53, this term emphasizes that the tomb was freshly carved from living rock and had never been used. The multilingual glosses (cut-in-rock, tallada-en-roca, taillé-dans-le-roc) reflect the technical precision of the Greek, highlighting both the tomb's construction method and its status as a costly, honorable burial place befitting royalty.

gloss_terse: Laodicean, inhabitant or church member of Laodicea
gloss_readable: This adjective identifies people or things associated with Laodicea, an important city in the Lycus Valley of Asia Minor. In Colossians 4:16, Paul refers to a letter circulating among the Laodiceans, indicating active Christian communities in the region. Laodicea was later one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, known for its wealth and tepid faith.

senses.1: Paul's reference in Colossians 4:16 to the Laodicean church and a letter they possessed shows early Christian networks in western Asia Minor. The multilingual evidence preserves the geographical-ethnic designation with minimal variation, recognizing Laodicea as a significant center in apostolic Christianity and early church correspondence.

gloss_terse: throat, larynx, gullet
gloss_readable: This anatomical term designates the throat or larynx, the upper part of the windpipe used in vocalization. In classical Greek, it referred both to the physical structure and metaphorically to speech or appetite. Paul quotes Psalm 5:9 in Romans 3:13, using this word in a vivid metaphor about human corruption: 'Their throat is an open grave.'

senses.1: In Romans 3:13, Paul employs this term within a catena of Old Testament quotations to depict universal human sinfulness. The image of the throat as an open sepulcher suggests speech that spreads death and corruption. Cross-linguistic glosses (throat, garganta, gosier, Kehle) render the straightforward anatomical sense, though the metaphorical force depends on understanding ancient imagery of speech and moral corruption.

gloss_terse: Lasea, a coastal city in Crete
gloss_readable: Lasea was a minor port city on the southern coast of Crete, near Fair Havens. It appears only in Acts 27:8 during Paul's voyage to Rome, where the ship stopped before attempting the dangerous autumn journey westward. Archaeological identification remains uncertain, though the general location near modern Kali Limenes is accepted.

senses.1: Mentioned in Acts 27:8 as a geographical reference point during Paul's perilous sea journey, Lasea marks where the voyage became increasingly dangerous due to approaching winter. The multilingual glosses preserve the name with slight orthographic variations (Lasaia, Lasáia, Lasea), reflecting standard practices for rendering Greek place names otherwise unknown in historical records.

gloss_terse: to burst open, split apart violently
gloss_readable: This verb describes a sudden, violent rupture or bursting, originally used for things that crack, split, or explode with force. Classical usage included the cracking of bones, crackling of fire, or bursting of objects under pressure. In Acts 1:18, it describes the gruesome death of Judas Iscariot, whose body burst open in the field purchased with his betrayal money.

senses.1: Acts 1:18 employs this graphic verb to describe Judas' death: falling headlong, he burst open and his intestines spilled out. The multilingual evidence (burst-open, reventó, éclater) captures the violent, sudden rupture implied by the Greek. This account differs from Matthew's hanging narrative, though both emphasize Judas' tragic end and the field's association with blood money.

gloss_terse: remnant, what remains after others are taken
gloss_readable: This noun denotes what is left over after a portion has been removed or destroyed—a surviving remnant or residue. In biblical theology, it carries theological weight as the concept of the faithful few who remain after judgment. Paul uses it in Romans 11:5 to describe Jewish believers in Christ as a remnant chosen by grace, echoing Old Testament prophetic themes.

senses.1: In Romans 11:5, Paul argues that just as in Elijah's day God preserved a remnant of seven thousand faithful Israelites, so in Paul's era there exists a remnant according to the election of grace. The multilingual glosses (remnant, remanente, reste, Rest) consistently render the sense of a surviving portion, connecting to the broader biblical theology of the faithful few preserved through divine purpose.

gloss_terse: smooth, level, even
gloss_readable: This adjective describes surfaces that are smooth to the touch, level terrain, or calm seas—anything lacking roughness or unevenness. In Luke 3:5, John the Baptist's ministry is described using Isaiah 40:4, where rough ways will be made smooth as preparation for the Lord's coming. The term suggests the removal of obstacles and the creation of easy passage.

senses.1: Luke 3:5 quotes Isaiah's prophecy that rough places shall become smooth paths, part of the dramatic landscape transformation heralding messianic arrival. The multilingual evidence (smooth, lisos, uni, λείας) captures the physical quality of evenness, though the prophetic context invests it with spiritual significance—the leveling of barriers and preparation of hearts for God's visitation.

gloss_terse: ministering, serving, liturgical
gloss_readable: This adjective describes something related to service or ministry, especially in religious contexts. It derives from 'leitourgia' (public service, liturgy) and denotes that which serves or ministers. In Hebrews 1:14, angels are called ministering spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation, emphasizing their functional role in God's purposes.

senses.1: Hebrews 1:14 applies this term to angels, defining them as ministering spirits dispatched for service on behalf of believers. The cross-linguistic evidence (ministering, servidores, dienend) uniformly emphasizes the active service dimension. This stands in deliberate contrast to Christ's superiority in Hebrews 1—while angels serve, Christ reigns as Son.

gloss_terse: scales (on eyes or skin), flakes, layers
gloss_readable: This noun denotes thin, flake-like layers that peel or fall away—originally describing fish scales, onion skins, metal fragments, or anything that forms in layered plates. In Acts 9:18, scales fall from Saul's eyes after Ananias prays for him, restoring his sight. Whether literal or metaphorical, the image conveys the removal of blindness and the reception of divine illumination.

senses.1: Acts 9:18 records that after Ananias laid hands on Saul, something like scales fell from his eyes and he regained sight. The multilingual glosses (scales, escamas, écaille) preserve the physical imagery, likely metaphorical for spiritual blindness removed. This dramatic moment marks Saul's transformation from persecutor to apostle, with restored sight symbolizing new spiritual perception.

gloss_terse: Levitical, pertaining to the tribe or priesthood of Levi
gloss_readable: This adjective designates what belongs to or relates to the Levites, the priestly tribe descended from Levi. In Hebrews 7:11, it specifically refers to the Levitical priesthood established under Mosaic law. The author of Hebrews uses this term while arguing that the old priesthood was imperfect, requiring replacement by Christ's superior priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.

senses.1: Hebrews 7:11 questions whether perfection could come through the Levitical priesthood, since the law was based on it. This sets up the argument for Christ's superior, eternal priesthood. The multilingual evidence (Levitical, levítico, lévitique, levitisch) uniformly identifies the adjectival form relating to Levitical office, central to the book's theology of Christ superseding the old covenant ministry.

gloss_terse: forgetfulness, oblivion
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the state of having forgotten or the condition of oblivion. In classical Greek, it personified forgetfulness and named a mythical river in Hades whose waters caused loss of memory. In 2 Peter 1:9, it describes the spiritual blindness of those who lack Christian virtues—they have forgotten the cleansing from their former sins.

senses.1: Second Peter 1:9 warns that believers lacking spiritual qualities are nearsighted to the point of blindness, having fallen into forgetfulness of their purification from past sins. The multilingual glosses (forgetfulness, olvido, λήθην, Vergessen) capture the cognitive lapse Peter describes. This forgetfulness represents not mere absent-mindedness but a dangerous spiritual amnesia about one's identity in Christ.

gloss_terse: nonsense, idle talk, rubbish
gloss_readable: This noun dismisses something as worthless chatter, futile nonsense, or empty words deserving no serious attention. Classical usage applied it to trivial matters, foolish speech, or things considered useless. In Luke 24:11, the apostles initially regarded the women's resurrection report as nonsense, reflecting ancient prejudices about women's testimony and the sheer incredibility of the claim.

senses.1: Luke 24:11 records the apostles' initial response to the women's Easter morning report: their words seemed like nonsense, and the men did not believe them. The multilingual evidence (nonsense, delirio, baliverne) captures the dismissive contempt implied. This moment highlights both the unexpected nature of resurrection and the cultural barriers the first witnesses had to overcome.

gloss_terse: receiving, taking, acceptance
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the act of receiving or accepting something, whether gifts, payments, or other transfers. In commercial contexts, it referred to receipts or takings. Paul uses it in Philippians 4:15 within an accounting metaphor, noting that no other church shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving except the Philippians.

senses.1: Philippians 4:15 employs financial terminology, contrasting giving and receiving to describe the unique partnership between Paul and the Philippian church. The multilingual glosses (receiving, recibir, λήμψεως, Empfang) reflect the commercial dimension of the term. Paul's careful language acknowledges their material support while framing it theologically as partnership in gospel ministry.

gloss_terse: freedman, a manumitted slave
gloss_readable: This Latin loanword designates a freed slave, someone who had been enslaved but was granted or purchased manumission. In Acts 6:9, it identifies a synagogue of the Libertini (Freedmen) in Jerusalem, likely composed of freed Jewish slaves or their descendants from various regions. Such synagogues organized along ethnic or social lines were common in the Second Temple period.

senses.1: Acts 6:9 mentions the Synagogue of the Freedmen among those disputing with Stephen. These were likely Jews who had been enslaved (perhaps by Romans) and later freed, or their descendants. The multilingual glosses (Freedmen, Libertînos, Libertins) preserve the Latin designation, reflecting the social reality of manumission in the Roman world and the diverse composition of Jerusalem's Jewish population.

gloss_terse: Libya, region in North Africa west of Egypt
gloss_readable: Libya designated the North African region west of Egypt, particularly the coastal areas known to the Greco-Roman world. In ancient geography, it often referred broadly to the African continent beyond Egypt. Acts 2:10 mentions Jews from the parts of Libya around Cyrene among those present at Pentecost, representing the widespread Jewish diaspora.

senses.1: Acts 2:10 includes Libyan Jews among the international crowd at Pentecost who heard the gospel in their own languages. The reference to 'the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene' specifies the Cyrenaica region, an important area of Jewish settlement. Cross-linguistic evidence (Libya, Libýes, Libye) preserves the ancient geographical designation for this North African territory.

gloss_terse: stone pavement, mosaic or tessellated floor
gloss_readable: This term describes a pavement made of fitted stones, particularly elaborate mosaic or tessellated work. In John 19:13, it designates the place called 'The Stone Pavement' (in Aramaic, Gabbatha) where Pilate sat on the judgment seat to pronounce sentence on Jesus. Archaeological evidence suggests this was a paved courtyard area in the praetorium.

senses.1: John 19:13 identifies the Lithostrotos as the specific location where Pilate rendered his verdict on Jesus. The term's architectural precision—referring to fitted stone paving—matches archaeological findings of Roman administrative spaces. Multilingual glosses (Stone-Pavement, Empedrado, Lithostrotos, Steinpflaster) preserve both the descriptive and transliterated forms, marking this as a historically significant site in the passion narrative.

gloss_terse: Linus, a Christian in Rome greeted by Paul
gloss_readable: Linus was a Christian believer in Rome mentioned alongside Claudia and others in Paul's greetings from 2 Timothy. Early church tradition identified him as an early bishop of Rome, though this connection is uncertain. The name was common in the Greco-Roman world, originally associated with a mythical minstrel in Greek legend.

senses.1: Second Timothy 4:21 includes Linus among the Roman Christians sending greetings to Timothy. Early church fathers like Irenaeus listed a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, though whether this is the same person remains debated. The multilingual evidence preserves the name with minimal variation, recognizing Linus as part of the apostolic-era Christian community in the imperial capital.

gloss_terse: luxurious, costly, sumptuous things
gloss_readable: This adjective describes what is rich, luxurious, or characterized by expensive refinement. Originally applied to oily or shiny objects, it came to denote sumptuous living and costly goods. In Revelation 18:14, it describes the luxurious and splendid things Babylon desired, now lost forever in her judgment—emphasizing the transient nature of worldly wealth.

senses.1: Revelation 18:14 pronounces that the fruit Babylon's soul longed for has departed, and all her luxurious and splendid things have perished. The multilingual glosses (luxurious-things, suntuosas, précieux, kostbar) capture the sense of expensive indulgence. This judgment oracle uses commercial language to depict the collapse of a system built on materialism and exploitation.

gloss_terse: southwest wind or direction
gloss_readable: This noun designates the southwest wind, one of the named directional winds in ancient Mediterranean navigation. In Acts 27:12, it appears in a navigational description of Fair Havens harbor, which faced southwest and northwest. Ancient mariners distinguished winds by direction, and this term specified the warm southwest wind common in the Mediterranean.

senses.1: Acts 27:12 uses this term to describe the harbor orientation at Fair Havens in Crete during Paul's voyage. The navigational precision reflects Luke's careful attention to seafaring details. Multilingual glosses vary between directional (southwest, suroeste) and regional (Lycie) interpretations, though the meteorological-geographical sense of the southwest wind or direction is primary in this context.

gloss_terse: eloquent, learned, skilled in speech
gloss_readable: This adjective describes someone accomplished in speech, learning, or rhetoric—eloquent and persuasive in communication. In classical usage, it denoted both learned scholarship and oratorical skill. Acts 18:24 applies it to Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew who was both learned in the Scriptures and powerful in speech, though initially knowing only John's baptism.

senses.1: Acts 18:24 introduces Apollos as an eloquent man, well-versed in the Scriptures. Alexandria was famous for its intellectual tradition, and Apollos embodied that heritage. The multilingual evidence (eloquent, elocuente, éloquent) emphasizes rhetorical skill, though the term also suggests broader learning. Priscilla and Aquila's instruction of Apollos shows that eloquence without full gospel knowledge needs correction.

gloss_terse: to quarrel about words, engage in verbal disputes
gloss_readable: This verb means to fight or wrangle over words, engaging in contentious disputes about terminology or semantics rather than substance. It suggests futile argumentation that generates heat rather than light. In 2 Timothy 2:14, Paul warns against this practice, which he says ruins the hearers and accomplishes nothing beneficial.

senses.1: Second Timothy 2:14 instructs Timothy to charge believers before God not to engage in word-battles, which profit nothing and lead to the ruin of listeners. The multilingual glosses (quarrel-about-words, discutir-sobre-palabras, λογομαχεῖν, Wortstreit) capture the contentious, unproductive nature of such disputes. Paul consistently warns against verbal controversies that distract from gospel truth and Christian character.

gloss_terse: word-battles, disputes about words
gloss_readable: This noun denotes quarrels or controversies focused on words and semantics rather than substantive truth. It describes the activity of logomachia—fighting over terminology, definitions, or verbal formulations in ways that obscure rather than clarify. First Timothy 6:4 associates such word-battles with the diseased craving for controversy characteristic of false teachers.

senses.1: First Timothy 6:4 describes false teachers as having a morbid craving for controversy and disputes about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, and evil suspicions. The multilingual evidence (word-battles, disputas-de-palabras, λογομαχίας, Wortstreit) emphasizes the combative, unedifying nature of such arguments. Paul sees these verbal contests as symptoms of spiritual disease rather than genuine pursuit of truth.

gloss_terse: Lycaonia, inland region of south-central Asia Minor
gloss_readable: Lycaonia was a plateau region in south-central Asia Minor, inhabited by a distinct ethnic group with their own language. Important cities included Lystra, Derbe, and Iconium. Acts 14:6 mentions Paul and Barnabas fleeing to the Lycaonian cities during their first missionary journey, encountering both hospitality and hostility in this culturally mixed frontier region.

senses.1: Acts 14:6 records Paul and Barnabas fleeing persecution in Iconium to reach the cities of Lycaonia—Lystra and Derbe. This region's cultural distinctiveness is evident in Acts 14:11, where locals spoke Lycaonian after witnessing Paul's miracle. The multilingual glosses (Lykaonia, Lykaonía, Lycaonie) preserve the geographical designation for this inland Anatolian territory, significant in early Christian mission expansion.

gloss_terse: in the Lycaonian language
gloss_readable: This adverb indicates speech in the Lycaonian language, the native tongue of Lycaonia distinct from Greek or Latin. Acts 14:11 records that after Paul healed a lame man in Lystra, the crowd shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form. This linguistic detail reveals the cultural gap between the apostles and the local population.

senses.1: Acts 14:11 notes that the Lycaonian crowd spoke in their native language, which Paul and Barnabas evidently did not immediately understand, leading to confusion about the sacrifice preparations. The multilingual glosses (in-Lycaonian, en-Lykaonistí, Lycaonien) preserve the adverbial form indicating language medium. This detail highlights the linguistic diversity of the ancient world and the challenges of cross-cultural gospel proclamation.

gloss_terse: Lycia, coastal region in southwestern Asia Minor
gloss_readable: Lycia was a mountainous coastal region in southwestern Asia Minor, known for its distinctive culture and federation of city-states. The region included important ports like Patara and Myra. Acts 27:5 mentions Paul's ship sailing across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia until reaching Myra in Lycia during his voyage to Rome.

senses.1: Acts 27:5 records that Paul's ship reached Myra, a major port in Lycia, during the perilous journey to Rome. Lycia was strategically located on Mediterranean trade routes. The multilingual glosses show some variation (Lukia, Lykía, Lystre) reflecting textual or geographical uncertainties, though Lycia as the southwestern Anatolian coastal region is the standard identification for this stage of Paul's sea journey.

gloss_terse: to ravage, devastate, destroy violently
gloss_readable: This verb describes violent destruction or devastation, originally used for the destructive cleaning work of fullers but extended to any ruinous damage. In Acts 8:3, it characterizes Saul's persecution of the church before his conversion—he was ravaging the church, entering house after house, dragging off men and women to prison.

senses.1: Acts 8:3 employs this vivid verb to describe Saul's pre-conversion persecution: he ravaged the church, invading homes and imprisoning believers. The term's violent intensity captures Saul's zeal as a persecutor. Multilingual glosses (was-ravaging, asolaba, dévaster) reflect the destructive force implied, making his later transformation to Paul the apostle all the more dramatic and evidence of grace's power.

gloss_terse: Lysanias, tetrarch of Abilene in Luke's chronology
gloss_readable: Lysanias was the tetrarch of Abilene, a small territory northwest of Damascus, mentioned in Luke's careful dating of John the Baptist's ministry. Luke 3:1 places John's prophetic emergence in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Lysanias governed Abilene. Historical evidence confirms a Lysanias ruling this region in the period Luke describes.

senses.1: Luke 3:1 includes Lysanias among the rulers anchoring the chronology for John the Baptist's ministry. By naming multiple secular authorities—Roman, Herodian, and local—Luke establishes precise historical context. The multilingual glosses preserve the proper name with standard variations, recognizing Lysanias as the historical tetrarch of Abilene whose governance provides temporal framework for gospel events.

gloss_terse: release, loosing, dissolution (especially from marriage)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a loosing or releasing from bonds, whether literal chains, moral obligations, or legal relationships. In 1 Corinthians 7:27, Paul uses it in the context of marriage, asking whether one has been released from a wife. The term's root meaning involves untying or setting free from a binding commitment.

senses.1: First Corinthians 7:27 poses parallel questions: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek marriage. Paul's counsel addresses the 'present distress' and prioritizes undivided devotion to the Lord. The multilingual glosses (release, separación, délivrance, Loesung) capture the sense of dissolution or freedom from marital bond, though Paul's point is contentment in one's present state.

gloss_terse: it is profitable, it is better, it pays
gloss_readable: This impersonal verb expresses that something is advantageous, profitable, or better—it pays or benefits. Classical usage often appeared in commercial contexts or ethical deliberations about what course of action yields benefit. Jesus uses it in Luke 17:2 in a severe warning: it would be better for someone to have a millstone around their neck than to cause a little one to stumble.

senses.1: Luke 17:2 contains Jesus' sobering statement that it would be more profitable (less disastrous) for an offender to be drowned than to cause a believer to sin. The multilingual glosses (it-is-better, conviene, il-vaut-mieux) capture the comparative sense. Jesus' hyperbolic warning emphasizes the gravity of leading others astray, measuring eternal consequences against even the most violent physical death.

gloss_terse: redeemer, deliverer, ransomer
gloss_readable: This noun designates one who liberates captives by paying ransom or effecting deliverance. It carries both commercial connotations (purchasing freedom) and theological significance (divine rescue). In Acts 7:35, Stephen applies it to Moses, whom God sent as both ruler and deliverer to Israel, prefiguring Christ's greater redemptive work.

senses.1: Acts 7:35 describes Moses as the one Israel rejected, yet God sent him as both ruler and redeemer through the angel in the burning bush. Stephen's speech highlights Israel's pattern of rejecting God's appointed deliverers. The multilingual glosses (redeemer, redentor, libérateur) capture the liberation theme central to Exodus and early Christian typology, seeing Moses as foreshadowing Christ the ultimate Redeemer.

gloss_terse: Lois, grandmother of Timothy
gloss_readable: Lois was the maternal grandmother of Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker. Second Timothy 1:5 commends her sincere faith, which she passed to her daughter Eunice and grandson Timothy. Her Jewish faith and Scripture instruction laid the foundation for Timothy's later Christian ministry, illustrating the multi-generational transmission of godly heritage.

senses.1: Second Timothy 1:5 recalls the sincere faith that dwelt first in Timothy's grandmother Lois, then in his mother Eunice, and now in Timothy himself. Paul's affectionate reference honors the faithful women who shaped Timothy spiritually. The multilingual glosses preserve the name with minimal variation, recognizing Lois as exemplifying the vital role of grandmothers in spiritual formation and the continuity of faith across generations.

gloss_terse: Maath, ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
gloss_readable: Maath appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, positioned between Mattathias and Naggai in the post-exilic lineage. Like many names in this section, no additional historical information survives beyond the genealogical record. The name may derive from Hebrew roots, though its etymology and historical identification remain uncertain.

senses.1: Occurring once in Luke 3:26, Maath represents one link in the ascending genealogy tracing Jesus back through post-exilic Judaism to David and ultimately Adam. The multilingual evidence uniformly treats this as a transliterated personal name, with consistent rendering across languages reflecting the name's obscurity in historical records beyond this genealogical context.

gloss_terse: Magadan, a place near the Sea of Galilee
gloss_readable: Magadan was a location on or near the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in Matthew 15:39 after Jesus fed the four thousand. Its exact site remains unidentified, though it may be related to Magdala. The parallel passage in Mark 8:10 has 'Dalmanutha,' suggesting these may be variant names for the same region or nearby localities.

senses.1: Matthew 15:39 states that after dismissing the crowds, Jesus got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. Textual variants and parallel accounts create uncertainty about the precise location. The multilingual glosses (Magadan, Magadán) preserve the name, recognizing it as a Galilean coastal district, possibly identical with or near Magdala, though ancient geographical precision remains elusive.

gloss_terse: magic, sorcery, occult arts
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the practice of magic or sorcery, originally referring to the religious teachings of Persian Magi but extended to occult arts generally. In Acts 8:11, Simon Magus had amazed the Samaritans with his magic arts for a long time, leading them to give him attention. The term reflects the widespread practice of magic in the Greco-Roman world.

senses.1: Acts 8:11 explains that Simon had astonished the Samaritans with his magic for a considerable time, causing them to regard him as 'the Great Power of God.' The multilingual glosses (magic-arts, magias, magie) capture the occult dimension. Simon's subsequent encounter with Peter reveals the incompatibility between genuine spiritual power and manipulative magical practices, even when practitioners seek to acquire Christian power.

gloss_terse: practicing magic, performing sorcery
gloss_readable: This participle describes someone actively engaged in practicing magic or sorcery. It denotes the ongoing activity of a magician or sorcerer employing supernatural or occult techniques. Acts 8:9 introduces Simon with this participle, identifying him as one who had been practicing magic in the city and amazing the Samaritan people.

senses.1: Acts 8:9 presents Simon as a man who had been practicing magic in Samaria, astonishing the population and claiming to be someone great. The multilingual evidence (practicing-magic, practicando-magia, pratiquer-la-magie) emphasizes the active, ongoing nature of his sorcery. This characterization sets up the dramatic contrast when Simon encounters genuine apostolic power and seeks to purchase the Holy Spirit's gifts.

gloss_terse: Magog, nation allied with Gog in eschatological battle
gloss_readable: Magog appears in Genesis 10:2 as a descendant of Japheth and in Ezekiel 38-39 as a people allied with Gog in an end-time invasion of Israel. Revelation 20:8 employs the names symbolically for nations deceived by Satan after the millennium, gathered for final battle against God's people. The identification remains debated, with suggestions ranging from Scythians to symbolic representation of hostile nations.

senses.1: Revelation 20:8 uses Gog and Magog to represent the nations from the four corners of the earth gathered for eschatological warfare against the saints. Drawing on Ezekiel's prophecy, John employs these names symbolically for end-time opposition to God's kingdom. The multilingual glosses preserve the proper name, recognizing Magog as part of apocalyptic imagery for forces arrayed against divine purposes.
